name: Feizhuliu (非主流)
blurb: China's 2000s "non-mainstream" teen style: Martian script, sad captions, 45-degree selfies
title: What Was Feizhuliu (非主流)? China's 2000s Non-Mainstream Style
description: Feizhuliu (非主流, "non-mainstream") was a Chinese teen style of the late 2000s: side fringes, 45-degree selfies, sad captions and Martian script on QQ Zone.
answer: Feizhuliu (非主流, literally "non-mainstream") was a youth style on the Chinese internet in the mid-to-late 2000s, mostly among teenagers born in the late 1980s and 1990s: eye-covering side fringes, wide-eyed selfies taken from a 45-degree angle above, usernames and captions in "Martian script" (火星文), and melancholy posts on QQ Zone. It had no founder or fixed start date, and it faded in the early 2010s as its teens grew up and platforms changed. Today it is mostly remembered with affectionate self-mockery, a bit like Western emo or scene kids.

ul: Hair: a long side fringe over one eye, dyed or spiky hair
Selfies: shot from above, eyes wide, lips pouted or a V sign, often with the line "look up at the sky at 45 degrees and the tears won't fall"
Images: photo-booth style frames, sparkly animated GIFs, grainy high-contrast edits with text on top
Words: screen names, status lines and blog posts in Martian script, about loneliness and heartbreak
Look: heavy eyeliner, skulls and crosses, earrings, partly borrowed from Japanese visual kei and punk

body: It spread through QQ Zone (Tencent's blog and photo space), QQ groups and forums, with images reposted so often that their origins are long lost.
Martian script (火星文, huoxingwen) means writing "Earthlings can't read". It started in Taiwanese chat and online games and spread to Hong Kong and mainland China.

It swapped common characters for rare look-alikes or sound-alikes and traditional forms, mixed in Zhuyin phonetic symbols, Japanese kana, Latin letters and numbers (520 for "I love you"), dropped strokes on purpose, and scattered symbols through sentences. Online converters turned normal text into it. It also drew criticism: Shanghai in 2006 barred such non-standard writing from official documents and media.

Shamate (杀马特), a transliteration of "smart", is often mentioned alongside feizhuliu, and the two overlap in hair and naming styles. Shamate is usually linked to young migrant factory workers and to more extreme hair and online "family" groups, while feizhuliu is associated more with students, selfies and sad text. The line between them was always blurry.
Chinese media at the time were mostly critical. Looking back, commentary is much kinder, often describing it as a generation's clumsy, low-budget search for identity just as the internet arrived.

Nothing ended it officially. Its teenagers grew up, smartphones and beauty-filter cameras changed how selfies looked, and Weibo and WeChat replaced QQ Zone for many. Today feizhuliu turns up as nostalgia and jokes about digging up your old QQ Zone, and as a deliberate retro reference in photos and styling.

faq.q: What does "45 degrees looking up at the sky" mean?
faq.a: A feizhuliu catchphrase: if you tilt your head up at 45 degrees, your tears won't fall. It went with upward-gazing or side-profile selfies to signal gentle sadness.

faq.q: Is feizhuliu the same as emo?
faq.a: Not exactly, but it is the closest Western comparison: a teen style built on a look, sad lyrics and posts, and a dedicated online space.
Roughly the mid-to-late 2000s, peaking among teens then in middle and high school, and fading in the early 2010s. No exact start date is documented.
